newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed weaker across the board after a wave of arbitrage trade selling against the arabicas market. The November contract lost $25 to close at $1,520 while other positions were around $23-24 weaker. There was also occasional origin selling from Asia and possibly Africa.

In New York arabica futures fell to a fresh one-month low as an increasingly bearish fundamental outlook prompted commodity funds to liquidate long positions. With the 1996/97 harvest well underway in top grower Brazil and beginning in Colombia and Central America funds had little incentive to hold on to long positions. Moreover, the Colombian 1995/96 crop will be higher than anticipated which also weighed on prices. Another bearish factor was that Brazil's Senate voted to repeal the ICMS export tax on certain commodities, including coffee.

COLOMBIA - According to Jorge Cardenas, president of the National Coffee Federation, coffee production in 1995/96 (October/September) will reach 12.5 million 60-kg bags up from earlier estimates of 11.5 million bags but still below initial estimates of 13.5 million bags. Cardenas said that rain had damaged the 1995/96 crop.

BRAZIL - The Brazilian Senate approved a bill making exports of primary commodities and some semi-manufactured goods exempt from the so-called ICMS export tax. This brought optimism to exporters but caution to roasters who fear an increase in domestic prices.

Exporters expect the new legislation to help increasing sales at a time Brazilian exports are usually higher due to the ongoing harvest. In August Brazil exported 1.54 million 60-kg bags, the largest volume of the year.

According to industry sources the 1996/97 coffee crop can be estimated at 24.5 million 60-kg bags, which in their view would not be sufficient to meet ACPC export commitments of 15 million bags and domestic demand of nearly 14 million bags by roasters and the soluble coffee industry.

In addition, the elimination of the export tax is likely to trigger a dispute among exporters and growers on prices, it was said. Exporters will back a drop in prices while producers will seek a price rise.

UNITED STATES - At a board meeting of the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on September 11 it was decided not to accept a recommendation to reduce the speculative position limit on the coffee 'C' futures. Earlier the Exchange said its coffee committee recommended the board slash the speculative position limit on coffee 'C' futures from 500 to 200 lots during a contract's delivery period.

JAPAN - Japan imported 498,973 bags of coffee in July 1996, 9.8 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 3.176 million bags, 1.9 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 fell by 11.9 per cent to 5.324 million bags.

Major suppliers of green coffee in January/July 1996 were Guatemala (202,600 vs 244,500 bags), Brazil (535,800 vs 738,400 bags), Colombia (683,300 vs 591,700 bags) and Indonesia (526,500 vs 394,300 bags).

NEW ZEALAND - New Zealand imported 93,000 bags of coffee in January/July 1996 15.2 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 rose slightly to 149,500 bags up from 148,100 bags the previous year.

Major suppliers of green coffee in January/July 1996 were Indonesia (15,600 vs 20,900 bags), Vietnam (18,800 vs 13,500 bags) and Papua New Guinea (14,600 vs 12,200 bags). Additionally the country imports quite a bit of solubles from Australia (14,800 vs 11,600 bags).
